chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: The day Roosevelt died on 52nd Street
summary: At the Onyx the musicians refused to play when Roosevelt died, and John Levy had to tell Jones the news.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: No, not right off hand. That goes back so far. We were all on 52nd Street, and we were always getting in discussions in between sets, and I think -- this was when Franklin Roosevelt died, the President, you know?

And Charlie Parker was able to -- he really was quite together on those kind of -- in those areas. You know? We all were depressed about Roosevelt's death, you know, because at that point he was like the father of the country, you know?
And when he died gee whiz, everybody felt bad, you know?
Did Charlie -- you say Charlie was together. In what way did he react to President Roosevelt's death?

Oh, he was let down, you know. But we still had to play our music. And then we were at -- oh, let me -- okay, now this is all coming back to me. We were working at the Onyx Club, still with Stuff Smith, or Ben Webster by this time, because I think Roosevelt died in '45 or '46.
And the club owner let the doors stay open
in case he wanted to get some business, and we just refused to play. Nobody went on the stand. We went home, you know?

And I'll never forget John Levy saying -- I didn't know. I hadn't had the radio on all day or anything, and John Levy just looked at me and said, "Man, do you know your President is dead?" I said, "What President?" I thought he was talking about the President of the union or something. You know?
He said, "No, Franklin Roosevelt died." You know? And I just kind of -- like somebody putting a pin in a baloon. I said, gee whiz, that's all I'd ever known was the President.
Yeah. We grew up -- it was like flag and country and Roosevelt. They were all sort of interchangeable.
